lessons.title: Terminal vs shell; bash vs PowerShell
lessons.body:
A TERMINAL is the window. A SHELL is the program inside it that runs what you type.
Common shells:
  bash / zsh   on macOS and Linux (and WSL on Windows)
  PowerShell   on Windows
They do the same job with different syntax. For elite-lab:
  - the TOOL itself is Python - `python3 elite.py` runs the same everywhere.
  - the mission commands are mostly bash/Unix (grep, nmap, john, sudo, gcc).
So use a Unix shell: macOS Terminal, any Linux terminal, or WSL on Windows
(install once: `wsl --install`). The PowerShell-specific material lives in the
'windows-ps' module, for Windows and Active Directory work.
Rule of thumb: bash for the missions; PowerShell when a lesson says PowerShell.

lessons.title: The terminal basics you actually need
lessons.body:
The PROMPT ($ on bash, > on PowerShell) waits for a command. A command line is:
  program   options(flags)   arguments
  nmap      -sV              127.0.0.1
Flags tweak behavior: short like -v, long like --verbose; combine short ones: -la.
Arguments are what it acts on (a file, a host, a URL).
Move around the filesystem:
  pwd   where am I        ls    list what's here       cd dir   go into dir
Paths: /  = root,  ~  = your home,  .  = here,  ..  = one level up.
Running & stopping: press Enter to run; Ctrl-C to stop a running command; `clear`.
Lifesavers: Up-arrow re-runs your last command, Tab auto-completes names, and
`<command> --help` (or `man <command>`) shows how to use it.
Quote anything with spaces or symbols: elite ask "what is idor".

lessons.title: grep - find lines that match
lessons.body:
grep searches text for a pattern and prints the matching lines. That's it.
  grep error app.log            lines containing 'error'
  grep -i error app.log         -i = ignore case (Error, ERROR too)
  grep -r TODO .                -r = search every file under here
  grep -n error app.log         -n = show line numbers
  grep -v error app.log         -v = INVERT: lines WITHOUT 'error'
  grep -c error app.log         -c = just count the matches
  grep -E 'cat|dog' file        -E = regex (here, cat OR dog)
The magic is piping - feed another command's output into grep with |:
  ps aux | grep ssh             running processes, filtered to ssh
In security this is 80% of log analysis - exactly what wire-01 and hunt-01 are.

lessons.title: curl - talk to a URL from the terminal
lessons.body:
curl makes web requests and prints what comes back. Your browser without the window.
  curl http://site/page         fetch the page body
  curl -I http://site           -I = headers only (HEAD request)
  curl -v http://site           -v = verbose: see the whole request/response + TLS
  curl -L http://site           -L = follow redirects (3xx)
  curl -o out.html http://site  -o = save to a file
  curl -d 'user=a&pw=b' http://site/login   -d = POST this form data
  curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer X' http://api   -H = add a header
curl is how you inspect what a server really sends, test an API, or check an endpoint
- the first tool you reach for on the App layer.

lessons.title: Piping them together
lessons.body:
The Unix idea: small tools chained with |, each doing one thing. Examples:
  curl -s http://site | grep -i 'password'     fetch a page, show password lines
  curl -sI http://site | grep -i server         just the Server: header
  grep -rn 'api_key' .                          hunt hardcoded secrets in a codebase
-s makes curl silent so the pipe is clean. Chaining curl + grep + sort + uniq is the
difference between staring at data and answering a question with it.

lessons.title: How AI coding tools use grep & curl
lessons.body:
When an AI coding assistant (like the one that built this repo) works in a codebase,
it mostly uses the SAME commands you just learned:
  - grep / ripgrep (rg): before changing code it searches the repo for where a
    function or string is defined and used, so it edits the right place. 'Find every
    use of parse_packet' is just grep.
  - curl / HTTP fetch: to read docs, test an API, or check a local server responds.
It isn't magic - it reads with grep, fetches with curl, runs code, reads the output,
and decides the next step. The tools are the same; watching the loop teaches you the
workflow.

quiz.q: For the hands-on missions, which terminal should a Windows user use?
options: WSL (a Unix shell) or PowerShell per the lesson
quiz.why: Mission commands are bash/Unix - use WSL; PowerShell for the windows-ps material.
Flags/options tweak how the program runs; the target is the argument.

quiz.q: How do you stop a command that's currently running?
Which grep flag searches all files in a directory tree?
How do you fetch ONLY the response headers with curl?
quiz.why: -I sends a HEAD request: headers only.

quiz.q: When an AI coding tool needs to find where a function is used, it most likely...
options: greps the codebase for the name
quiz.why: It searches (grep/ripgrep) for the symbol - same tool you just learned.
